mappings.note: Which feeling the Tai-Mitthu bond shows (mamta aur sneh) -- LO-8 is that emotional relationship by name, not LO-7's loneliness theme.
What value Jagan Master's opening of the cage signals (karuna, naitikta) -- his idea of freedom, C-1.1-LO-10.
What Mitthu's flight stands for (the wish to be free). This is the cage-as-symbol reading, C-1.2-LO-3, rather than Jagan Master's stated principle in LO-10.
The root of Tai's sorrow: distance from family and absence of talk -- the samvaadheenta and loneliness problem, LO-7.
Which social malaise the story exposes (akelapan) -- LO-7.
Which 'naiya' Tai means and why she says it -- her isolation and the burden of getting through life alone, LO-7.
What 'slowly everything passed into other hands' points to -- the household's decline after the family left for the city, LO-9.
Why all Tai's mamta poured onto Mitthu -- the emotional bond, LO-8.
What her new interest in whose chillies and guavas are ready reveals about her -- the change the bond worked in her, LO-8.
Jagan Master's character with examples -- his principles and idea of freedom, LO-10.
For whom the title 'Samvaadheen' fits best, with reasons -- the speechlessness/isolation theme, LO-7.
Why the big house is called a soona khandahar -- the ruin as symbol, C-1.2-LO-3, which names khandahar directly.
Answer-given item: Mitthu supported Tai's loneliness / who gifted him. The content is the Tai-Mitthu bond, LO-8.
Answer-given item: Mitthu had flown before Tai returned -- the escape that drives the realistic ending, LO-10.
Answer-given item: the villagers feared the shock the truth would give Tai -- the deception behind the ending, LO-10.
Can creatures really grow used to a cage? Give examples from around you. A reasoned personal position, C-2.1, not the symbolic reading of C-1.2-LO-3.

Find one more example each of the story's devices. The named set includes punarukti and atishayokti (C-1.2-LO-4); C-1.2 is added for chitratmakta and samvadatmakta, which no LO lists. NOTE: this item is duplicated as the next one.
Duplicate of the previous item, with the device table printed in full: punarukti and atishayokti give C-1.2-LO-4, chitratmakta and samvadatmakta the competency C-1.2.
Which category the ending belongs to and what new ending you would write -- LO-10 asks exactly for a view on the realistic ending.

Why the character is never named, only 'mastarain' or 'Jagan Master ki gharwali'. Naming a woman by her husband's relation is language shaping identity -- C-4.3 at competency level; LO-5 is idioms and LO-6 bird-love, so neither applies.
Research the Kumbh: why it is held and when the last and next fall. Respect for the cultural material the text carries, C-4.2.
Why the sons and daughters-in-law left the village and what they must have felt -- urban migration and its effect on village life, LO-9.

Imagine the real Mitthu returns and continue the story. Creative composition, C-2.2 at competency level: LO-6 asks for an EXISTING prasang recast as dialogue, and this invents a new one; LO-5 is Tai's letter or self-narration.
Go home and ask an elder how they spent their time at your age, then write it down. The activity is aimed straight at the samvaadheenta theme (LO-7) and is carried out as reasoned expression (C-2.1).
Write the lost-and-found advertisement Jagan Master would place. Functional composition, C-2.2 at competency level -- an advertisement is neither the letter of LO-5 nor the dialogue of LO-6.
List idioms that mention an animal, starting from 'apne munh miyan mitthu banna' -- the muhavare and lokoktiyan outcome, C-4.3-LO-5.

From the paragraph find an antonym, an idiom, a verb, a noun, a pronoun, an adjective, a karak and a karta. A grammar and word-class drill, so the language-skill competency C-4.1, not a literature outcome; C-3.2-LO-2 is the nearest sibling but covers shabd-yugm and sentence types, which this does not ask.
Classify sentences by meaning -- vidhanvachak, nishedhvachak, prashnavachak and the rest. C-3.2-LO-2 names vaakya-bhed by meaning exactly.

Assign emotions to groups and present them as mime. Expression, but neither C-2.1 (reasoned argument) nor C-2.2 (written composition) fits a wordless performance, so the oral-and-written-expression goal CG-2 is cited.
If you could fly like Mitthu, where would you go and why -- reasoned personal expression, C-2.1.
Find out about the food preferences of the women in your home and how often they are cooked -- a social issue explored and expressed, C-2.1.
Compose riddles whose answers are tota, Tai, Kumbh, pinjra, kamra, Ganga -- language play built on the text, the language-skill competency C-4.1.

The word 'tota' across Eighth Schedule languages plus the sentence in your mother tongue -- Indian linguistic diversity, C-4.3 at competency level and CG-4. Not C-4.3-LO-6, which is about bird-love passages, nor LO-5, about idioms.
Who wrote 'Samvaadheen'. Authorship recall, no LO states it, so C-1.1 at competency level.
Shekhar Joshi's birthplace. Biographical recall, C-1.1 at competency level.
What Tai sighs at the opening -- 'how will the boat cross?', her loneliness, LO-7.
Mitthu answers 'Ram-Ram kaho, Sitaram kaho'. The bird's devotional speech is where bird-love and cultural identity meet in language -- C-4.3-LO-6, rather than plain recall of the bond.
What the big house once held -- family, servants and cattle; the baseline against which migration is measured, LO-9.
Why the sons and their wives left -- they became city people. Urban migration, LO-9.
How Tai lit the hearth for herself alone -- 'do joon ka ek joon'. LO-7 for the solitary life it describes, C-3.2-LO-1 because the answer rests on a lokdharmi turn of phrase that carries the setting.
What Mitthu did while Tai told her ram-kahani -- the patient listener, the bond, LO-8.
How the two quarrelled -- Mitthu upsetting the bowls; the texture of their relationship, LO-8.
What Tai cursed him with and what he threw back -- their exchange, LO-8.
What she did with Mitthu before going out to an invitation -- her protectiveness, LO-8.
When her dharm-sankat arose: the Kumbh trip, because of Mitthu. The dilemma exists only because of the bond, LO-8.
The objection that Mitthu would need his own train ticket -- part of the same dilemma over the bird, LO-8.
Who resolved her worry and how -- Jagan Master's wife agreeing to keep Mitthu; the arrangement made for the bird, LO-8.
What Tai was doing on the day of departure -- petting Mitthu and weeping, LO-8.
Assertion-reason on Jagan Master's free thinking and his unease at a caged bird -- his concept of freedom, LO-10.
Statements about Jagan Master -- his unease at the cage and the Gita-Rahasya; LO-10.
What the big house was like: a soona khandahar -- the ruin image, C-1.2-LO-3.
Fill in: he had made certain niyam-siddhant for himself -- the principles behind his idea of freedom, LO-10.
How to view the decision to fetch a substitute parrot -- a judgement on the story's realistic close, LO-10.
Which book he was reading (Gita-Rahasya) -- the detail that characterises his idealism, LO-10.
The story's central message: the loneliness of old age and family speechlessness -- LO-7.
Why the big house is called a soona khandahar -- the ruin symbol, C-1.2-LO-3.
How Ganpat helped Tai -- by bringing her Mitthu, which begins the bond, LO-8.
What changed in Tai's life once Mitthu came -- the bond and its effect, LO-8.
Why Mitthu is called a sharp-witted pupil -- he learned what Tai taught him; the bond's daily texture, LO-8.
Duplicate of the previous item (same stem; this copy also has the answer and stray options of another question bleeding into it). Same mapping: LO-8.
Mitthu would not leave the open cage -- the caged bird that no longer wants out is the cage symbol, C-1.2-LO-3.
Fill in: he scattered grain from the cage door outward -- Jagan Master acting on his principle of freedom, LO-10.
How many days he kept it up (three or four) -- his persistence in freeing the bird, LO-10.
Mitthu's eye fell on the open roshandan -- the moment his freeing succeeds and backfires, LO-10.
The sense of 'all the idealist's parrots flew' -- his ideals and plans came to nothing, LO-10.
What Jagan Master did after the escape -- calling through the orchard, drenched in sweat; the consequence of his principle, LO-10.
The village's dread of Tai's return -- the pressure that produces the substitute parrot and the realistic ending, LO-10.
Statements on Ganpat's substitute-parrot plan and keeping Tai deceived -- the ending, LO-10.
Why Tai told Mitthu her ram-kahani. She pours out her life to a bird because there is no one else -- the speechlessness problem, LO-7, rather than the bond itself.
When the nok-jhonk between them happened -- the bond's texture, LO-8.
Why the Kumbh trip became a dharm-sankat -- she could not leave Mitthu, LO-8.
Which problem Jagan Master's wife solved -- the care of Mitthu, LO-8.
Why Jagan Master tried to get Mitthu out of the cage -- his conviction about freedom, LO-10.
Why Mitthu did not come out the first time -- habituation to the cage, the symbol, C-1.2-LO-3.
How Mitthu got away through the roshandan -- the event that tests Jagan Master's principle, LO-10.
Ganpat's suggestion after the escape and his reason -- the substitute that makes the ending what it is, LO-10.
Why Jagan Master tried to teach the substitute parrot -- sustaining the deception, LO-10.
The fall of the big house and how the family scattered -- urban migration and its effect on village life, LO-9.
Describe the dawn exchange between Tai and Mitthu and its importance -- the bond, LO-8.
What Tai felt leaving Mitthu before the Kumbh -- the bond, LO-8.
Assertion-reason: she would not light a fire for herself but cooked dal-bhaat for Mitthu -- the bond, LO-8.
What she came to know of after Mitthu arrived -- whose chillies and guavas were ready; the bond drew her outward, LO-8.
What kind of pupil Mitthu is likened to -- kushagra buddhi; the teaching relationship, LO-8.
Fill in: he began his lesson to wake Tai from her bhor ki jhapki -- the daily bond, LO-8.
The words Mitthu wakes her with -- 'Har Har Gange! Sitaram bol!'. Devotional speech taught to a loved bird, C-4.3-LO-6, language and cultural identity.
The blessing Tai gives him -- 'jeete raho beta, jug-jug jio', addressing a bird as a son. C-4.3-LO-6.
What Mitthu returns for the blessing -- 'khush raho!'. The same bird-love-in-language, C-4.3-LO-6.
Statements on 'ab kaise kategi?' answered by 'kategi! kategi!! kategi!!!' and the life it gave her -- punarukti and its effect, C-1.2-LO-4.
Which story Tai told in the drowsy afternoon -- the saga of past wealth and standing, which measures what migration cost, LO-9.
